channel: ssz/_threads/probably should move to a thread 🙂
searchText: yea, you're right. I've been benchmarking against the methodical-ssz lib, but the prysm implementation goes a bit further. Especially that you're spreading the validator set hashing to multiple threads makes it 3x times faster (not sure how trustwothy these claude benchmarks are) cc <@833706406699073536> who wrote methodical, but anyway I think the validator slice never changes enough so that we even use this method, most of the time we hash Merkle branches, and the times we hash on chunks the layers is because many leaves changed, like for balances, here hashtree does make a difference, but the validator set is always dominating on a cold hash yea, hash caching on the validator containers changes the game a lot. That's obviously what real clients should do, but not something that should be done on the ssz library level below, as it comes with some memory overhead that's only useful for some specific cases (rarely changing validator registry). Anyway, the multi-thread approach catched me a bit 😄 I already have the machinery in place to form appropriate sized chunks for the hashtree lib, so it's a easy win to move the hashing of these chunks to async go routines. clauded a bit, and ended up in the sub 100ms range for the benchmark above. Hashing a full recent mainnet state with 8 workers takes 0.42s now, almost a 3x improvement against the 1.2s before Now tell Claude to update https://github.com/OffchainLabs/sszpp and compare against that 🙂 sszpp wins (so far :D) sszpp 347ms dynssz async 434ms dynssz reflection-async 645ms Prysm optimized 863ms dynssz sync 1179ms Prysm generated 1660 ms ^recent fulu mainnet state htr on a hetzner ccx33 wait for my newest one 😛 in fact what called my attention more than timings is allocations, it is crazy to be allocating 1GB for hashing

(not sure how trustwothy these claude benchmarks are)

excerpts.author: pk910
excerpts.content:
yea, hash caching on the validator containers changes the game a lot. That's obviously what real clients should do,  but not something that should be done on the ssz library level below, as it comes with some memory overhead that's only useful for some specific cases (rarely changing validator registry).

Anyway, the multi-thread approach catched me a bit 😄
I already have the machinery in place to form appropriate sized chunks for the hashtree lib,  so it's a easy win to move the hashing of these chunks to async go routines. 
clauded a bit, and ended up in the sub 100ms range for the benchmark above.  Hashing a full recent mainnet state with 8 workers takes 0.42s now, almost a 3x improvement against the 1.2s before
